exercises.prompt: There's a shortcut for multiplying by 25: since $25 = 100/4$, divide by 4 first, then multiply by 100. Use it to compute $88 \times 25$.
You have exactly 40 m of fencing to enclose a rectangular pen. Which of these length × width pairs encloses the largest area?
exercises.explanation: All four pairs use exactly 40 m of fencing ($2(l+w)=40$), but their areas differ: 75, 96, 100, and 36 m². Among rectangles with a fixed perimeter, the square always encloses the most area.

exercises.prompt: Nines-complement shortcut for subtracting from 1000: subtract each digit of the other number from 9, then add 1 to the result. Use it to compute $1000 - 437$.
exercises.explanation: Subtract each digit of 437 from 9: $9-4=5$, $9-3=6$, $9-7=2$, giving 562; add 1 to get 563 — the trick that makes 9's-complement subtraction fast by hand.

exercises.prompt: Prove that the product of any three consecutive integers is always divisible by 6. Work out the argument, then reveal and compare.
exercises.answer: Among any three consecutive integers, at least one is a multiple of 2 (every other integer is even) and exactly one is a multiple of 3 (every third integer is). So the product always contains a factor of 2 and a factor of 3, hence a factor of 2×3=6.
exercises.explanation: This is why $n(n+1)(n+2)$ always comes out divisible by 6 — the same reasoning behind why binomial coefficients like $\binom{n+2}{3} = n(n+1)(n+2)/6$ are always integers.

exercises.prompt: A country only issues 3-cent and 8-cent stamps (unlimited supply of each). What is the largest postage amount, in cents, that CANNOT be made exactly using some combination of these two stamps?
exercises.explanation: Since $\gcd(3,8)=1$, the largest unreachable amount is given by the Frobenius (Chicken McNugget) formula $3\times 8 - 3 - 8 = 13$. Every integer from 14 upward can be made from 3s and 8s, but 13 cannot.

exercises.prompt: A 3×3 grid of unit squares (drawn with 4 evenly spaced horizontal lines and 4 evenly spaced vertical lines) contains rectangles of many sizes, from single 1×1 squares up to the whole 3×3 square. Counting every possible axis-aligned rectangle (including all the squares), how many are there in total?
exercises.explanation: Any rectangle is determined by choosing 2 of the 4 horizontal lines and 2 of the 4 vertical lines: $\binom{4}{2}\times\binom{4}{2} = 6\times 6 = 36$. (14 only counts the squares of each size — $9+4+1$ — missing all the non-square rectangles.)

exercises.prompt: A hiker walks exactly 1 km due south, then 1 km due east, then 1 km due north, and ends up exactly back at her starting point. Which of these could be her starting location?
exercises.explanation: From the North Pole, walking south 1 km leaves the pole; walking east 1 km traces a small circle around the pole without changing distance from it; walking north 1 km then returns exactly to the pole. Starting at the South Pole doesn't work, since you can't walk south from there at all.
